passage: Lalit, beta, listen. I'm your grandfather, Chaitanya. When I was ten, a boy named Bhau used to flick my ears every day at the school gate, and my fists curled so tight my nails left marks. I wanted to hit him once, hard, so he would stop. I lay awake planning it. But I had seen another boy caught fighting: the headmaster's scolding, a letter home, a bleeding lip. So one morning I walked away and stood with Rohit and the others near the water tank. Then I told our class teacher, who listened, said it was not my fault and spoke to the headmaster that same day. It was slow, but it worked. And the planning stopped eating my nights. I learned that anger is fair, but it should not drive.

qa.q: Where did the boy flick Chaitanya's ears every day?
qa.a: He flicked his ears at the school gate.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya walk away instead of hitting the boy?
qa.a: He had seen another boy caught fighting and punished and hurt, so he feared the same for himself.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do besides walking away, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: He stood with friends near the water tank and told the class teacher, which slowly worked and ended his night-time planning.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel on hearing that Grandfather Chaitanya once wanted to hit someone?
qa.a: Lalit may feel relieved that angry feelings are normal, since Chaitanya calls the anger fair, and the story also shows what to do with them.

grounding: An elder recalls wanting to hit back at a bully, then walking away, staying near friends and reporting it.

passage:
Thursday
Today Rocky knocked my tiffin off the bench AGAIN and everyone laughed. My hands shook. I wanted to punch him so hard he'd never do it again. In maths I planned exactly how I'd get him back tomorrow. I couldn't even hear the teacher.
At break Sabina saw my face. "Don't. You'll be the one in trouble, and he's bigger." She walked with me, and we stayed next to her group.
After lunch we went to Sharma Sir together and I told him. He wrote it down and called Rocky to the staffroom straight away. Sir said I was right not to hit.
My fists still feel tight. But I'm not planning anything anymore.
Tushar

qa.q: What did Rocky knock off the bench?
What was Tushar feeling during maths?
qa.a: Tushar felt furious and wanted revenge, so full of anger that the teacher's voice was lost.

qa.q: Why was walking away with Sabina and telling Sharma Sir wiser than hitting back?
qa.a: Hitting could have got Tushar punished or hurt, while staying near friends and reporting made the teacher step in that same day.

qa.q: How might Sabina have felt seeing Tushar's face at break?
qa.a: Sabina may have felt worried that Tushar would fight and get hurt or in trouble, so she stayed close.

grounding: A child wants to hit back at a bully and plots revenge, then walks away with a friend, stays near friends and reports it to a teacher.

passage:
Every evening at the village cricket patch, Bunty grabbed Lalit's bat and threw it into the thorn bushes. Lalit's jaw locked. On the walk home he kicked stones and planned it: tomorrow he'd shove Bunty into the canal ditch in front of everyone.
His sister Bhavna walked beside him. "You're doing the stone thing again. What's he done?"
Lalit told her, and the plan too.
"He's twice your size. You'll get hurt, and Baba will hear you started it." She hooked her arm in his. "Tomorrow we play near the temple steps with my friends. And tonight you tell Baba."
That night Baba listened, then said he'd speak to the sarpanch and to Bunty's father the next morning.

qa.q: Where did Bunty throw Lalit's bat?
What was Lalit feeling on the walk home?
qa.a: He felt angry and wanted revenge; his jaw locked and he kicked stones while planning to shove Bunty.

qa.q: What did Bhavna suggest that was safer than revenge?
qa.a: She suggested playing near the temple steps with her friends and telling Baba that night, instead of fighting a bigger boy.

qa.q: How might Baba see what Lalit tells him?
qa.a: Baba takes it seriously and wants adults to handle it, planning to speak to the sarpanch and Bunty's father.

grounding: A boy bullied at cricket wants to hit back and plots revenge; his sister reminds him fighting could hurt him, suggests staying near friends, and he reports it to their father.
